newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Mandela opens new sphere of influence for S. Africa.
newsitem.headline: Mandela opens new sphere of influence for S. Africa.

text.p: President Nelson Mandela, opening a new sphere of influence for South Africa's young democracy, said on Monday he had agreed to commit troops to an international peace effort in Central Africa.
In a television interview marking the halfway point of his five-year presidency, Mandela said he had given the undertaking to former Tanzanian president Julius Nyerere last week.
"I indicted that I am prepared to send to troops to that region, but there is certain specific information which I want before I can decide what size of military unit I should send."
Mandela said he would send officials to the region to gather the information, but he added: "In principle I am prepared to contribute troops."

Nyerere briefed Mandela on a summit of East and Central African leaders who decided last week that a neutral force should be created to provide safe corridors for aid to more than a million refugees from ethnic violence in Rwanda and Burundi.
The force would help Rwandan refugees now in eastern Zaire to return to their home country and escape fighting between rebels and Zairean government forces.
Last week South Africa suspended an 87 million rand ($18.5 million) arms contract with the Rwandan government because of the fighting in the region.
Mandela had previously refused to participate in military operations abroad, saying his country's democracy was too young and its newly integrated army too inexperienced.
He confirmed he was "very angry" last year when General Sani Abacha of Nigeria executed political opponents in the midst of a South African initiative to save them.
In an apparent renewal of his unsuccessful call a year ago for European and U.S. sanctions against Nigeria, he said trade, rather than diplomacy, was the most effective weapon.
"Moral authority alone can never influence policies of governments. It is the country that trades with...Nigeria that can influence the policy of that country," he said.
Mandela, 78, said in a joint interview with state television and CNN that his government had done well given the challenges it inherited in 1994 after 300 years of white domination.
He said he had warned during the campaign for the country's first all-race elections that it could take a decade to begin to deliver the fruits of democracy.
"I warned that this is not an event, it is a process. We have been planning....we are in the process of carrying out our plans. We are delivering," he said.
The key to South Africa's recovery from the effects of apartheid lay in generating economic growth, he said.

"We have been able to turn a negative growth rate into a positive growth rate in two and a half years...but we will not be able to make a dent in this large army of unemployed until we reach growth of six percent," he said.

Responding to contradictory reports about his comments at a closed meeting of the National Executive Committee of his ruling African National Congress (ANC), Mandela denied he had withdrawn support for Deputy President Thabo Mbeki as his successor.

Mandela said it was not his job to choose who filled his shoes, but he added:"If the organisation elected Thabo Mbeki I would fully support that. He is highly capable, smart, influential and committed.
"I have no doubt that any of the leaders of the ANC would produce results far above what the present incumbent (Mandela) has achieved," he said.
